topics.title: The security mindset
topics.technical: Security is thinking about how systems fail on purpose: assets, threats, attack surface and trust boundaries. The defender must cover everything; the attacker needs one gap — which is why systematic thinking beats ad-hoc patching.
topics.simple: Learning to see the ways things can be broken, so you can guard them.

topics.title: The CIA triad
topics.technical: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability define what security protects: keeping secrets, preventing tampering, and staying up. Every control maps to one or more; every incident violates one or more.
topics.simple: The three things security defends: secrecy, correctness, and being online.

topics.title: Networking for security
topics.technical: Attacks travel over IP, ports, DNS and TCP/HTTP; reading packets, ports and status codes separates a probe from noise. You cannot defend a network you cannot picture.
topics.simple: Understanding how data moves so you can spot when something moves wrong.

topics.title: Linux and the command line
topics.technical: Most security tooling and most servers are Linux: file permissions, processes, logs and shell scripting are the daily surface for both attacker and defender. The terminal is the arena.
topics.simple: The command line is where both attackers and defenders actually work.

topics.title: Cryptography basics
topics.technical: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing and digital signatures provide confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. Using primitives correctly matters more than understanding their internals — rolling your own is the classic fatal error.
topics.simple: The math that keeps secrets and proves identity — and why you must never invent your own.

topics.title: Authentication and passwords
topics.technical: Systems verify identity with passwords, tokens and multi-factor auth; passwords must be salted and hashed with slow functions, never stored or logged. Credential handling is where most breaches begin.
topics.simple: Proving who you are, and storing passwords so a stolen database is useless.

topics.title: Access control
topics.technical: Authorisation decides what an authenticated user may do: least privilege, role-based access, and ownership checks on every action. Missing authorisation — not broken crypto — is the commonest serious flaw.
topics.simple: Being logged in is not permission for everything — each action must be checked.

topics.title: Web vulnerabilities: the OWASP Top 10
topics.technical: Injection, broken auth, XSS, insecure deserialisation and access-control flaws recur across the web. Knowing the top ten by name lets you find and fix the bugs attackers look for first.
topics.simple: The ten mistakes attackers try first on every website.

topics.title: SQL injection
topics.technical: Untrusted input concatenated into queries lets attackers rewrite them, reading or destroying data. Parameterised queries — never string-building — close it entirely; this single lesson prevents a whole disaster class.
topics.simple: Letting user input become part of a database command — and the one-line fix.

topics.title: Cross-site scripting
topics.technical: XSS injects attacker script into pages other users view, stealing sessions and acting as them. Output encoding and Content-Security-Policy are the defences; every unescaped user string is a candidate.
topics.simple: Sneaking malicious code into a page so it runs in a victim's browser.

topics.title: Secure coding practices
topics.technical: Validate input at trust boundaries, encode output, handle errors without leaking, keep secrets out of code, and patch dependencies. Security is a property of ordinary code written carefully, not a bolt-on.
topics.simple: Writing everyday code in the careful way that leaves fewer holes.

topics.title: Network security
topics.technical: Firewalls, segmentation, VPNs and TLS control who reaches what and protect data in transit. Defence in depth assumes any single layer will fail and plans for it.
topics.simple: Controlling who can reach which machines, and encrypting what travels between them.

topics.title: Reconnaissance and scanning
topics.technical: Attackers map targets with nmap, banner grabbing and OSINT before striking; defenders run the same tools to find their own exposed surface first. You cannot defend what you did not know was reachable.
topics.simple: Mapping a target's exposed doors and windows — done by both sides.

topics.title: Vulnerability assessment
topics.technical: Scanners and manual review find known weaknesses; CVSS scores severity, and prioritisation by real exposure beats patching alphabetically. Finding is easy; fixing what matters first is the skill.
topics.simple: Finding the weak spots and fixing the dangerous ones before the trivial ones.

topics.title: Penetration testing basics
topics.technical: Ethical hacking probes systems with permission through recon, exploitation and reporting, proving impact rather than listing theory. Authorisation and scope are the line between a pentest and a crime.
topics.simple: Breaking in on purpose, with permission, to prove what a real attacker could do.

topics.title: Malware and defence
topics.technical: Viruses, worms, ransomware and trojans spread and persist by known mechanisms; endpoint protection, least privilege and backups blunt them. Offline backups are the one control ransomware cannot encrypt.
topics.simple: How malicious software spreads — and why offline backups beat ransomware.

topics.title: Incident response
topics.technical: When defence fails, response limits damage: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn. A rehearsed plan and good logs turn a breach into an incident instead of a catastrophe.
topics.simple: A calm, practised plan for when something gets in — contain first, blame never.

topics.title: Logging and monitoring
topics.technical: Security visibility is logs, alerts and SIEM correlation; you cannot investigate what you did not record. Alerts must fire on real signals, not drown responders in noise.
topics.simple: You cannot catch what you never logged — record, watch, and alert on what matters.

topics.title: Social engineering
topics.technical: The human is the softest target: phishing, pretexting and baiting bypass technical controls entirely. Awareness, verification habits and least privilege limit the blast radius of a fooled employee.
topics.simple: Attacking the person, not the computer — and why training is a real control.

topics.title: Governance, risk and compliance
topics.technical: Security operates under policy and law: risk assessment, standards like ISO 27001, and regulations shape what must be done. GRC turns security from heroics into a repeatable, auditable programme.
topics.simple: The rules, standards and paperwork that make security a programme, not luck.

topics.title: The capstone
topics.technical: Assess a deliberately vulnerable application end to end: recon, find flaws, prove impact safely, and write a professional report with prioritised fixes. The report is the deliverable that gets security people hired.
topics.simple: One full security assessment, from finding holes to a report that gets them fixed.
